Garran Hill

Neo-Georgian.  Walter Hines Page.  110 years of remarkable stewardship.

The Arrival

It has stood here
since before the columns
were raised.

Some houses hold history. This one shaped it. Neo-Georgian architecture. Longitudinal plan. Columned portico. The proportions are correct because the original drawings survived.

Four bedrooms. Six baths. Seven fireplaces. 6,072 square feet. 4.15 acres.

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen.
The same men who built Pinehurst.

The Threshold

The door has been open
since 1916.

Original 1916 leaded glass sidelights and over-door fanlight at the front entry, preserved exactly as built. The hardware was specified in 1916. It has not been replaced. That is not maintenance. That is devotion.

The Interior

Two primary stair cores.
Three staircases.
One axis.

The foyer runs the full depth of the house. Original oak floors throughout. The proportions were drawn in 1915 and nothing has been changed that didn't need to be. Restored 1999–2001 by Thomas O'Shea.

"You cannot leave this room quickly."

The Library — Garran Hill

The Rooms

Fire going.
No one home yet.

Seven fireplaces. Six with propane gas logs. The drawing room Delft fireplace is original. Formal by proportion. Intimate by firelight. The sound that fills seventeen feet without effort.

The History

He named it Garran Hill.
He longed for it every day he was gone.

He bought the land in February 1913. He commissioned the design. He directed the craftsmen. Walter Hines Page, publisher, ambassador, son of the South, never slept here. He died December 21, 1918, before the house was finished.

Walter Hines Page  ·  1855–1918

Publisher. Ambassador.
The man who named
this hill.

Editor of The Atlantic. Co-founder of Doubleday. U.S. Ambassador to Great Britain during the First World War. He carried a letter of introduction from Woodrow Wilson and the homesickness of a man who had built something beautiful on Carolina soil that he would never see finished.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"

"In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest."

The Driveway — 110 years

The Grounds

4.15 acres.
The world outside
does not exist here.

Salt water pool, 20 × 40 feet, installed 2022. Twenty-eight irrigation zones fed by a 130-foot well. Rose garden. Boxwood. Mature canopy. Twelve parking spaces.

Someone still puts flowers on Blue Fox's grave.

It is ready for
the fifth family.
